name: Ivan Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that work for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Works for me. I'm on the board of our grain co-op, so I'm used to saying one thing in the meeting and another in the car park. I'll try to give you both.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent Ridgeway Farm from the county council, 180 hectares of wheat, beans and grass, with about 600 ewes and thirty beef cattle. Mornings are the sheep, then whatever field job the weather allows, and evenings are paperwork at the kitchen table. Lambing in March is the best and worst month of the year. The rent review letters are what really wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ana teaches at the primary school, and our two, Mateo and Sofia, are thirteen and ten. We bought Brook Cottage down the lane with a mortgage, so we're not living in the council's house, which was a deliberate choice. We've a decent cushion saved, more than a year of costs if we're careful, because the last five harvests were good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the drone salesmen: useful for some things, oversold for most. At the co-op I'd point out that the money never went to farmers anyway, it went to the people selling the kit. Online I'd probably just share a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the same pressures as now, no more, no less. The thing on my mind isn't AI, it's that the council keeps talking about selling off its farms to balance the books. My tenancy on Ridgeway Farm runs out in 2029, and no computer program worries me as much as the council's budget meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as I do, and I'd keep using the chat program now and then for grant forms, because it saves me an evening. I'd go to the council meetings with the tenants' group and push them to keep the estate public. And I'd keep the savings where they are, because a tenant always needs a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with that one itch. It's the same itch I've had for three years, so I'm used to scratching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the chat program for grant forms. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I paste in the government's hedge planting rules and ask it to help me fill the form for 400 metres of new hedge. It gets it about eighty per cent right and I fix the rest. Last spring that saved me two evenings, which I spent with Sofia at her netball instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the council does sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then a pension fund or a big estate buys it, and I'm one tenant they'd rather not have. I'd have a year's money and Brook Cottage, so we wouldn't starve. But I'd lose the business I've built over twelve years.

say: I'd say AI is **oversold**, like the drone salesmen were.
I'd tell the co-op the money always went to **kit sellers**, not farmers.
think: Nothing changes for me except the **same old pressure** from the council.
My **tenancy ends in 2029**, and that worries me more than any program.
do: Keep using the **chat program** for grant forms, saving an evening each time.
Go to council meetings with the **tenants' group** to keep the estate public.
Leave the **savings** untouched as a tenant's cushion.
feel: Mostly fine, with a familiar **itch** about the tenancy.
S0.quote: My tenancy on Ridgeway Farm runs out in 2029, and no computer program worries me as much as the council's budget meeting.
fieldNote: His worry predates AI: the **council's budget** could end his tenancy.
He uses AI **pragmatically** for forms and can say exactly what it saves.
His strong savings and own cottage mean a sale would hurt the **business**, not the family's survival.

steps.text: Keep farming Ridgeway and using AI for grant forms
Lobby the council with the tenants' group to keep its farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, it's real, and farmers should own the tools rather than rent them from a big company. At the co-op I'd be the one saying let's buy a robot weeder together before a contractor does. Online I'd post photos if it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one suits me. My office work is the part I hate, and if a program does the cattle passports, the grain contracts and the rent paperwork, I get my evenings back. The hands-on work stays mine for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what Jim at Hill End does with his farm software for a season, then copy what works. At the co-op I'd push for a shared robot weeder for the beans, split twelve ways. I'd also ask Ana to help me set up the accounts program properly over the Christmas holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but more interested than scared. It's like when the sheep handling crate came in: the sceptics came round once they saw it save their backs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your world would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grain merchant's office, honestly, two women who've done our contracts for years. If the buying and booking goes to software, those jobs shrink first. And Ana, a bit, because I hear the schools are already using AI to mark homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said this suits you. Is there a part that doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The data. If my farm software belongs to some company in another country, then they know my yields before my landlord does. I'd rather the co-op owned our farm data, because whoever owns the numbers ends up owning the farm.

say: I'd say farmers should **own the tools**, not rent them from big firms.
I'd urge the co-op to buy a **robot weeder** together.
think: This one **suits me**, because software takes the paperwork I hate.
The **hands-on work** stays mine for a good while.
do: Watch Jim at Hill End's **farm software** for a season, then copy what works.
Push the co-op for a **shared robot weeder**, split twelve ways.
Set up the **accounts program** with Ana over Christmas.
feel: A bit uneasy but more **interested** than scared.
S1.quote: I'd rather the co-op owned our farm data, because whoever owns the numbers ends up owning the farm.
fieldNote: Steady adopter: he waits for **a neighbour's proof**, then copies.
His progressive views show in wanting the **co-op to own** data and machines.
He worries for **office workers** at the grain merchant and for Ana's school.

steps.text: Copy Jim at Hill End's farm software after one season
Propose a shared robot weeder for the grain co-op
Keep the sheep and cattle work as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying the government has to step in, and fast, before the land market goes mad. At the co-op I'd be calling an emergency meeting. Online I'd be one of those people posting long threads, which Ana would tell me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the council would sell Ridgeway to whoever runs farms with robots, and they'd do it before my 2029 renewal. A pension fund with an AI manager doesn't need a tenant. I'd be a farmer with six hundred ewes, a year of savings and no farm to put them on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd stop any new spending on the farm, no new tractor, no new shed. I'd move as much as I can into savings and make sure Brook Cottage is safe. I'd get the tenants' group to the local paper and our MP, and I'd ask the union for farmers whether they've got legal help on tenancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightening, to be honest. I'm usually the calm one at the co-op, and I don't think I would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and robots about 3 years later. How does that gap play out for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap is the dangerous bit. In 2028 the AI does the planning, so a landlord can see on a screen which farm is worth more with a robot and no tenant. My hands are still useful till 2031, but the decision gets made in 2028, by someone looking at a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're safe, which would be true for money. I wouldn't tell them I don't know if they'll grow up on a farm. Mateo loves the lambing, so that would be a hard conversation.

say: I'd say the **government must step in** before the land market goes mad.
I'd call an **emergency co-op meeting** and post long threads online.
think: The council would sell **Ridgeway Farm** to a robot-run buyer before 2029.
I'd have **600 ewes**, a year of savings and no farm.
do: Freeze new farm spending: **no tractor, no shed** this year.
Move spare money into **savings** and protect Brook Cottage.
Take the tenants' case to **the MP**, the paper and union lawyers.
feel: Frightened, and no longer **the calm one** at the co-op.
S2.quote: I'd be a farmer with six hundred ewes, a year of savings and no farm to put them on.
fieldNote: He sees the real threat as **landlord decisions** made in 2028, not robots in 2031.
Money is safe but the **business** he built is not.
He'd **shield the children** from his own doubts.

steps.text: Cancel the planned tractor and shed purchases
Move spare farm money into savings to protect Brook Cottage
Take the council tenants' case to the MP and local paper
Ask the farmers' union for legal help on tenancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to make sure robots work for farmers, not just for landowners. At the co-op I'd put a plan on the table for buying machines together. I'd say it loud at the council too, because public farms could be where this is done fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is just about enough if the co-op moves early and I renew in 2029. If the council keeps the estate, a tenant with shared robots can still make a living. If they sell, I'm in the same mess as the fast one, only later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for the 2029 renewal, maybe offering a longer lease at a higher rent. I'd put money into the co-op's machinery fund, say twenty thousand, once two or three neighbours have trialled the robot kit. And I'd use the AI properly for planning, not just forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy-to-worried. There's a plan, but it depends on people I don't control, the council most of all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on. What changes on the farm in 2031, before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning: what to plant, when to sell lambs, what to pay for feed. An AI doing that better than me is a bit humbling. I've been guessing lamb prices at the kitchen table for twelve years, and a computer will guess better by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put twenty thousand into the co-op fund. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, I'd just want to see it working first. If Jim's robot weeder survives one wet autumn at Hill End, I'll put my money in. If it sits broken in the yard, I keep my money in the bank.

say: I'd say we have five years to make robots **work for farmers**.
I'd tell the council **public farms** could show how to do this fairly.
think: Five years is **just enough** if the co-op moves early.
If the council **sells the estate**, it's the fast picture again, only later.
do: Bid for a **longer lease** in 2029, even at a higher rent.
Put **£20,000** into the co-op machinery fund after neighbours' trials.
Use AI for **farm planning**, not just grant forms.
feel: Uneasy-to-worried, because the plan depends on **the council**.
S3.quote: I've been guessing lamb prices at the kitchen table for twelve years, and a computer will guess better by 2031.
fieldNote: He has **real control** over the co-op, but not over the landlord.
His investment rule is clear: **see it survive** one wet autumn first.
He admits AI may plan **better than him**, without much bitterness.

steps.text: Offer the council a longer lease on Ridgeway Farm in 2029
Put £20,000 into the co-op machinery fund after trials
Use AI for lamb sales and crop planning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and it would be a disgrace to waste it. I'd tell the co-op we should become the robot owners in our valley. I'd be pushing the government for land reform too, so farms don't all end up with funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I think I'd be all right. I'd have the 2029 renewal done, ten years to see which machines actually work, and I'd be fifty-six when the robots are ready. My worry is less for me and more for whether the kids can ever afford land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd mostly watch and wait: keep farming, keep saving, let others make the early mistakes. Then from about 2034 I'd move with the co-op on shared machines. And I'd start an education fund for Mateo and Sofia so they have a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a little uneasy, because ten years of warning doesn't mean anyone uses it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything about the tenancy. With ten years, the council can't sell under me without a fight, and I'd have the renewal signed. In the fast one the robots and the AI arrive before I've even got the paperwork done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mateo loves lambing. What would you tell him about farming as a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn both ends: the animals and the machines. I'd tell my son Mateo that the farmers who survive will be the ones who can fix the robot and still deliver a lamb.

say: I'd call **ten years a gift** that would be a disgrace to waste.
I'd push for **land reform** so farms don't all go to funds.
think: I'd **be all right**, with the 2029 renewal done and time to choose machines.
My real worry is whether the kids can **ever afford land**.
do: Keep farming and **saving** while others make the early mistakes.
Join the co-op's **shared machines** from about 2034.
Start an **education fund** for Mateo and Sofia.
feel: Calmer, but still **a little uneasy** about whether anyone uses the time well.
S4.quote: I'd tell my son Mateo that the farmers who survive will be the ones who can fix the robot and still deliver a lamb.
fieldNote: Ten years removes his **tenancy panic** and lets his steady style work.
He shifts the worry onto **the next generation** and land prices.
His advice to Mateo blends **animals and machines**.

steps.text: Hold off on new machines until neighbours have tested them
Join the co-op's shared robot scheme from about 2034
Open an education fund for Mateo and Sofia

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the council would sell before I could renew, and twelve years of work would go to a fund with a robot. What would help is a rule that public farms stay public, and that tenants get first right to buy. Grants for co-ops to buy machines together would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the land, and that's the whole question. Robots don't scare me half as much as the man who will own the robots and the fields they work on.

headlineQuote: Robots don't scare me half as much as the man who will own the robots and the fields they work on.
portrait: Ivan is a **council tenant farmer** on Ridgeway Farm with 600 ewes, wheat and beans.
He has **strong savings** and his own cottage, but his tenancy ends in **2029**.
He is a **steady adopter** who copies neighbours once a tool has proved itself.
In every picture his real fear is the **landlord selling**, not the machines themselves.
With more warning he plans **co-op ownership** of robots and feels nearly safe.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the council would sell Ridgeway before he could renew.
whatWouldHelp: A rule keeping **public farms public**, with tenants' first right to buy.
Grants for **co-ops** to buy machines together.
